claims.text: The initial material is a cast, single-phase refractory HEA with a homogeneous BCC microstructure.
A nominally equiatomic CrMoNbTa alloy or a similar refractory HEA is typically used as an intermediate layer in plasma-facing components.
Exposure to molten Cu at approximately 1000 °C for 2–4 hours promotes selective liquid-metal infiltration and phase separation.
Cu infiltration produces a phase-separated, bicontinuous microstructure containing a continuous FCC Cu network in a refractory BCC HEA matrix.
The infiltrated material will contain only limited interfacial reaction layers while maintaining strong bonding between Cu and the HEA.
Differences in mixing enthalpy cause molten Cu to infiltrate selectively and segregate within the refractory HEA.
The continuous Cu network increases heat transfer through enhanced electronic and lattice thermal transport.
The residual refractory HEA matrix provides mechanical strength.
The residual refractory HEA matrix resists irradiation-induced swelling.
Controlled infiltration avoids deleterious interfacial reactions that would compromise structural integrity.
Cu infiltration will increase thermal conductivity by approximately 50–100% relative to the untreated monolithic HEA.
The infiltrated composite will retain mechanical strength comparable to that of the untreated HEA.
The infiltrated composite will retain resistance to irradiation-induced damage during thermal cycling up to approximately 800 °C.
The untreated refractory HEA has lower thermal conductivity than the proposed Cu-infiltrated composite.
The proposed performance should hold during cycling from room temperature to about 800 °C under moderate energetic He+ irradiation.
The proposed performance may fail at significantly higher irradiation doses or after extended thermal exposure above 800 °C.
Degradation of Cu–HEA interfacial bonding during long-term operation may invalidate the proposed performance.

contradictions.description: The intervention requires molten Cu but specifies processing at approximately 1000 °C, below Cu's ordinary-pressure melting point of about 1085 °C; as written, the stated temperature is inconsistent with a molten-Cu infiltration step.
